analytic.title: Work-in-Progress: Generating Counter-Examples to Schedulability Using the Schedule Abstraction

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Schedulability analyses check whether all tasks in a task set will meet their timing requirements. They thus provide a boolean answer. Some analyses may also compute bounds on the worst-case response-time (WCRT) of tasks. However, only knowing WCRT is often not enough to understand which tasks are involved in deadline-miss scenarios and under what conditions those scenarios may happen. Therefore, it is hard to infer what must be fixed to make unschedulable task sets schedulable. This issue is exacerbated when tasks are nonpreemptive since they are subject to timing anomalies that are non-trivial to analyze.

The schedule-abstraction technique is a relatively scalable reachability-based response-time analysis that explores the space of possible schedules to detect potential deadline misses. Therefore, it can tell which jobs (of which tasks) are involved in a deadline-miss scenario. However, the schedule abstraction framework is not yet able to provide concrete release and execution times (and therefore concrete schedules) for those jobs. The reason is that, to reduce memory consumption, the schedule abstraction framework deliberately forgets information about the job execution ordering that led to a state. It also merges states to defer state-space explosion during the state-space exploration. In this work, we propose a technique to derive concrete schedules resulting in deadline misses by augmenting the exploration phase of the schedule-abstraction technique to carry minimal extra information that allows resolving ambiguities while tracing back jobs involved in deadline-miss scenarios using our own partialorder planning algorithm.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Schedulability analyses are means of asserting timing correctness of real-time systems. However, they are often too focused on only answering that specific question, thus only providing a yes/no answer. Some analyses additionally derive bounds on the worst-case response-time (WCRT) of tasks in a given task set [1]. This provides additional insights on the system timing behavior but, when systems are deemed unschedulable by a test, WCRTs usually do not provide enough information to understand which tasks are involved in a deadline-miss scenario and under what conditions or arrival patterns that scenario occurs. This makes the process of debugging and redesigning/re-configuring a non-schedulable real-time system difficult and time-consuming. This problem exacerbates in non-preemptive task sets because they are susceptible to timing anomalies which are often hard to discover or anticipate.

While formal verification frameworks such as UPPAAL can generate counter-examples when a property is violated (e.g., a deadline miss happens) [2] and provide exact schedulability results, scalability issue w.r.t. the problem size (number of tasks and processing cores) have been shown for some types of schedulability problems [3]. As an alternative Nasri et al. [4]- [6] introduced a reachability-based response-time analysis technique, called schedule-abstraction graph (SAG), that efficiently explores the space of possible schedules and therefore can identify the set of jobs involved in a deadline miss scenario. SAG checks all possible schedules and find any deadline-miss scenario if one happens. However, SAG

is not yet able to provide concrete release and execution times (and therefore concrete schedules) for the jobs involved in a deadline-miss scenario because it deliberately forgets information about the job execution ordering to save memory, and merges states to reduce its search space. Both aspects are key to the scalability of the SAG and to make it faster than generic model checkers.

The goal of this work is to extract concrete execution scenarios (schedules) that result in a deadline miss when executing an unschedulable task set. To start, in this work, we focus on non-preemptive job sets (or periodic tasks) with release jitter and execution time variation scheduled by a joblevel fixed-priority scheduling policy (JLFP) on a single-core platform.

In this paper, we propose a three-step algorithm to build counter-examples when a task set is deemed unschedulable by the SAG analysis. The first two steps aim at limiting the search space for concrete execution scenarios that result in a deadline miss. The third step applies a partial-order planning algorithm on the reduced state-space to build a set of schedules that end up with a deadline miss.
We start the paper by rapidly introducing the schedule abstraction analysis (Section II). We then present our approach to extract counter-examples in Section III.

div.head: A. System Model
div.p: We consider the problem of scheduling a finite set of nonpreemptive jobs J on a single-core platform using a workconserving JLFP scheduling policy (e.g., Rate-Monotonic, Deadline Monotonic, or Earliest Deadline First, ...). The set of jobs J to analyze may be generated by considering all jobs released in a feasibility interval of a task set (e.g., two times the hyper-period added to the maximum offset for periodic tasks with offsets for example).

div.head: B. Introduction to the Schedule-Abstraction Graph
div.p: The schedule-abstraction framework performs a reachability-based analysis to derive bounds on the worst-case and best-case response times of the jobs and check the schedulability of a job set [4]. It efficiently explores the state-space of all possible execution scenarios of the job set by aggregating similar schedules into an abstraction that is focused on the ordering between the execution of the jobs. To do so, it builds a directed acyclic graph G = (V, E), called schedule-abstraction graph (SAG), where V is a set vertices and E a set of edges. Each edge e l ∈ E is labelled with a job J i ∈ J , and represents a scheduling decision made by the scheduler to dispatch job J i on the processor. Each vertex v p ∈ V represents a system state after a sequence of job dispatch decisions taken by the scheduler. A system state v p is represented by a set of jobs J p ⊆ J that have been dispatched until reaching state v p , and a processor availability interval [A min p , A max p ] where A min p is the earliest time at which the processor may potentially become available to execute a new job, and A max p is an upper-bound on the time at which the processor will certainly become available to execute a new job. In different words, the processor is certainly busy executing jobs of J p until A min p and is certainly free after A max p . Note that, given their definitions, A min p and A max p are also the earliest and latest time at which the last job dispatched by the scheduler until reaching state v p may finish its execution. Thus, let J i ∈ J p be the label of an edge ending in v p , if A max p > d i , then J i may miss its deadline and the job set is deemed unschedulable by the SAG analysis.
Fig. 1 shows a schedule-abstraction graph for the job set used as running example in this paper. The characteristics of the jobs are provided in Table I.

To defer the state-space explosion inherent to reachabilitybased analyses, whilst building the SAG, the schedule abstraction framework merges vertices that represent system states in which the same set of jobs have already been dispatched, and in which the processor availability intervals overlap. This is illustrated with v 4 in Fig. 1. Details on how the SAG is constructed may be found in [4], [5].

div.head: A. Challenges
div.p: There are several challenges to building a counter-example (i.e., a concrete execution scenario that ends in a deadline miss) using the schedule abstraction-analysis framework: Challenge 1. Because of the merge phase, more than one path in the SAG may lead to a deadline-miss state v m . Not all the sequences of dispatch decisions represented by those different paths may actually lead to a deadline miss. For example, in Fig. 1, there are two paths leading to the deadlinemiss state v 7 but as will be shown in Section III-E, only the path {J 1 , J 3 , J 2 , J 4 , J 5 } represents a sequence of job-dispatch decisions that ends in a deadline miss. The first challenge is thus to identify the subset of paths that actually result in a deadline miss. Challenge 2. A path in the SAG does not represent a single execution scenario (i.e., concrete release times and execution times of jobs executed on the processor). Instead, it represents a sequence of scheduling decisions that may be identical for many execution scenarios. Identifying which of those concrete execution scenarios actually lead to a deadline miss is our second challenge. Challenge 3. Possibly the most important challenge is related to one of the implementation choices of the scheduleabstraction framework. To reduce memory consumption, the framework 'forgets' most of the states that were visited during the construction of the SAG. It only keeps track of the leaves of the graph (i.e., states that still need to be expanded) and forgets the previously explored states. Therefore, when reaching a deadline-miss state, it does not remember which sequence(s) of job-dispatch decisions led to that state.

div.head: B. Proposed Solution
div.p: Our solution consists of three steps.

Step 1. Whenever a deadline-miss state v m is found when building the SAG, we first identify the subset of jobs X that may be involved in that deadline miss. Note that the set X may contain jobs that are not dispatched until the deadline miss but whose properties influenced the schedule of other dispatched jobs. We discuss this step in Section III-C.

Step 2. We build a reduced version of a subgraph of the SAG using the set of jobs X . We save all labelled edges of the reduced graph (i.e., the sequences of scheduling decisions that may have led to the deadline miss). Labels of vertices however are not saved. We discuss this step in Section III-D Step 3. Finally, we use the reduced SAG to build counterexamples using a backward partial-order planning algorithm. We explain that step in Section III-E.

div.head: C. Identifying Jobs Involved in the Deadline Miss
div.p: Our first step is to reduce the number of jobs we need to consider in the generation of a counter-example. The goal being to reduce the size of our search space.
We base this step on the following property of workconserving JLFP scheduling policies.
Property 1: Under a work-conserving JLFP scheduling policy, if the processor is idle at time t, then the schedule of jobs dispatched after t is not impacted by the jobs dispatched before t.

We use Property 1 as follows. Assume an edge e l ∈ E outgoing a vertex v p ∈ V of the SAG. Let J l be the job labelling e l , i.e., the job dispatched in system state v p . If the earliest release time r min l of J l is later than the latest availability time A max p of the processor, then the processor is certainly idle before executing J l . Thus, all jobs dispatched until reaching v p will not participate to a deadline miss occurring after v p .

Therefore, when building the SAG, for each state v p that is added to the graph, we divide the set J p of jobs dispatched until v p in two subsets, namely, the sets of jobs J p CE that were dispatched after the last certain idle time occurring until reaching system state v p , and the set of jobs dispatched before that idle time. Note that if there was no certain idle time until reaching v p , then J p CE = J p . Fig. 2 shows how the set J p CE evolves through the SAG on our running example. Thus, when we reach a deadline-miss state v m , we know that a counter-example may be generated considering execution scenarios where only jobs in J m CE execute, and where only jobs in X = J \ {J m \ J m CE } are released, i.e., all jobs but those dispatched before the last idle time.

div.head: D. Building a Reduced SAG
div.p: The second step uses the information carried by the job sets J m CE and X to build a smaller reduced SAG that encodes the reduced state-space that must be explored to build counterexamples.
To do so, we use three new lemmas. Lemma 1: The same deadline-miss state v m is reached in a SAG built from the full job set J or the reduced job set X .
Proof: By Property 1 and the fact that X contains all jobs in J except those dispatched before the last idle time before reaching v m .
Lemma 2: Any branch of the SAG containing a job that is not in J m CE can be removed from the graph since it will not lead to the deadline-miss state v m .
Proof: Since, by its definition, J m CE contains all jobs of X dispatched until reaching v m , no job outside of J m CE will be on a path to the deadline-miss state v m .

Lemma 3: Let J m be the job missing its deadline in the deadline-miss state v m . Any branch of the SAG containing J m and where J m does not miss its deadline can be removed from the graph since it cannot lead to the deadline-miss state v m .

Proof: Because J m may only be dispatched once on a path in the graph, if it does not miss its deadline on that path, then that path cannot reach the deadline-miss state v m in which, by definition, J m must have missed its deadline.

Using the three lemmas above and applying them to our running example, we get a reduced SAG as shown in Fig. 3. Note that the graph in Fig. 3 is a subgraph of the original SAG shown in Fig. 1. Furthermore, in both graphs, the same deadline-miss state is reached.

All the transitions (i.e., edges and their labels) are saved for the next step of our counter-example generation algorithm. The deadline-miss state v m is also recorded. However, the content of the intermediate states leading to v m do not need to be saved as they are irrelevant for the third step of our algorithm.

div.head: E. Building Counter-Examples
div.p: In the final step of our solution, we traverse the reduced SAG built at step 2 using a backward depth-first algorithm. This means that the algorithm attempts to build one complete counter-example at a time and as soon as at least one valid counter-example is found, the algorithm stops.

In short, let P be a path ending at the deadline-miss state v m in the reduce SAG. We start from the deadline-miss state v m and visit each system state on the path P until we either reach the initial state of the graph, or we prove that the path P cannot lead to a deadline miss at v m . In the former case, we found the sequence of scheduling decisions that ends up in a deadline miss at v m and we can stop. In the latter case, there must be another path P in the reduced SAG that also ends in v m and leads to a deadline miss. In that case, we choose a different path in the reduced SAG that was not entirely visited yet and apply the same approach until we find P .

When traversing a path P of the reduced SAG, we calculate the earliest and latest times at which each job on the path P may have started executing to ensure the last job J m on the path misses its deadline. The procedure is as follows.
Take the job J m that misses its deadline in v m . We know that J m must complete after its deadline d m . Since we also know that the processor certainly become available at A max

Fig. 4 shows an example of the backtrack algorithm applied on the reduced SAG of Fig. 3. The upper-path in Fig. 4 corresponds to the backtracking on path {J 2 , J 3 , J 4 , J 5 } of the graph in Fig. 3. It ends with EST DM 2 = 7 and LST DM 2 = 5, implying that there is no execution scenario in which J 2 may start executing before all other jobs and J 5 misses its deadline. However, a valid start interval is found for every job in the lower-path in the graph of Fig. 4, which corresponds to the backtracking on path {J 3 , J 2 , J 4 , J 5 } of the graph in Fig. 3. Path {J 3 , J 2 , J 4 , J 5 } with the computed start and finish times is a valid example of a family of schedules that ends in a deadline miss for J 5 .

div.head: IV. SUMMARY AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper, we presented a solution to derive concrete examples of execution scenarios that end in a deadline miss for unschedulable task sets. Our solution is based on an augmentation of the schedule-abstraction framework. We demonstrated how it may work for a set of non-preemptive sequential tasks scheduled by a JLFP scheduling policy on a single core platform. We plan on generalizing the proposed technique to the generation of counter-examples for more complex task models (e.g., limited-preemptive (conditional) DAG tasks, gang tasks, ...) executed in multi-core and distributed systems.
